One resonant plant, one fixed drive-power budget, and each excitation in common use:
the Fisher-optimal multisine, a naive cophased multisine, a swept sine, and
broadband and shaped noise. Selecting any of them updates two figures of merit, and the
full comparison table, in the browser with no install.

```{=html}

```

## The two axes

Every drive here spends the same total power. What differs is how it is distributed, and that
separates into two independent quantities:

- **Time to identify to 5%** — set by the drive's power spectrum $P_{xx}(f)$ alone. This is
  the Cramér–Rao bound (the same Fisher kernel as the [landing-page game](index.qmd) and the
  [`system_ident` pipeline](examples/interactive.qmd)). Concentrating power where the plant's
  modal parameters are least certain shortens the time by roughly 40× relative to a flat
  spectrum. Every flat-spectrum drive — flat multisine, white noise, a linear sweep — reaches
  the same time whatever its phase, because the Fisher information does not depend on phase.

- **Crest factor** — the peakiness of the drive, `max|x|/rms`. It matters because the actuator's
  DAC has a fixed range: a peaky drive clips, or forces the whole drive to be scaled down,
  discarding SNR. The Fisher-optimal drive is low-crest as a by-product — it collapses onto
  ~2 tones, so its crest is ~2 with nothing to tune. A swept sine is lowest (~$\sqrt2$, a
  constant-envelope sine); broadband noise sits ~3.4; and a naively cophased multisine
  reaches ~15, an impulse that would clip immediately. The lever for headroom is therefore the
  same as the lever for speed — concentrate the spectrum — rather than any phase adjustment
  (see the caveat below).

## Why the optimal spectrum is fastest

The best performer (★) is the Fisher-optimal spectrum. It collapses almost entirely onto
two tones (the whole budget sits on the two resonances — effective line count ≈ 2), and that
single property accounts for both results: it identifies the plant ~40× faster than any flat
drive, and two tones are intrinsically low-crest (~2), so it stays inside the actuator range
without further work. A swept sine matches that crest but spends power off-resonance;
broadband noise is slower and pays a further leakage / variance penalty for being aperiodic.
That is the case for [optimal excitation](tutorial/why-optimal-excitation.qmd), shown here
interactively rather than algebraically.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## A caveat on crest, and on phase adjustment
Crest is the quantity the DAC sees, and this page measures it on the raw synthesized
samples. In a real actuator the drive is shaped by the whitening / actuation chain on its way
to the DAC, which reassigns the per-frequency phases — so a crest minimized at synthesis (for
example by a Schroeder phase schedule) does not survive to where the range limit applies. The
dependable way to keep the drive within range is to keep its spectrum concentrated, which the
optimal design does regardless; phase-shaping is not a dependable lever here.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Running the real package
This page is a JavaScript approximation for interactive exploration. The
[Run it live](examples/interactive.qmd) page executes the actual `system_ident` package —
the real `optimal_excitation`, `TFModel`, and Cramér–Rao code, on a reduced aLIGO
suspension — in the browser through WebAssembly.
:::
